THE HISTORY OF ENGLISH COMMON LAW
units.text:
Bloody Beginnings
The history of English common law

units.label: slide 2
units.text:
Legal Basis 
Common law and Statute law are the two broad categories of law.
Common law is based on customs and judicial precedent 
Statute law has been passed by the legislature
Precedent is determining a verdict based on a previous case
Common law began in the 11th century in England

units.label: slide 3
units.text:
Common Law
As far back as the early 5th century, different Anglo-Saxon tribes lived in England
Each tribe had its own customs and laws
After the Norman invasion there was a lot of violence
If the murder could not be caught, the whole community was punished (taxes) 
This application of punishment only applied to a murder of  a Norman
By the late 1100s, this tax (fine) was applied to everyone

units.label: slide 4
units.text:
Policing
There was no police force at this time – community policing under the “Peace Pledge”
10 neighbors kept an eye on each other and pledged to obey the law, have good behavior, and detain and deliver the criminal
This evolved into the concept and position of a Reeve
Chosen by the serfs from among themselves

units.label: slide 5
units.text:
Duties of the Reeve
Make sure everyone worked and didn't cheat the landowners out of money
Sometimes a district or shire was administered by one reeve, so that person was referred to as the “shire reeve”
“Sheriff “

units.label: slide 6
units.text:
Typical Crimes 
Crime (ONF) literally meant sin
Abrecken – breaking another
Stalen – stealing
Husbreche – house breaking (theft)
Two wifing – bigomy 
Siblecker  - sibling lying (incest)

units.label: slide 7
units.text:
STOP
Arrêter – to detain/arrest
Arrest – “bring to a rest” i.e. stop someone from running away
Rest (OE) – lie down and sleep 
These two terms merged into the meaning we have today
Not only legal terms are a product of this mixing

units.label: slide 8
units.text:
Norman Invasion
William the Conqueror became the King
Set up a centralized government to look after the different territories
Shires became counties – local courts to deal with issues
Many legal terms were replaced with French words

units.label: slide 9
units.text:
The Court System
William I brought the idea of a court system
 Shire courts were replaced by county courts controlled by the King
The King had his own court (for serious crimes and criminals – barons and nobles)
The Normans created a church court as well
Issues of marriage, divorce, witchcraft, and heresy

units.label: slide 10
units.text:
Application of the Law	
William I chose justiciars (judges)  to travel to the counties to hear cases and settle disputes 
They would follow the laws of the local community
The villagers would meet with the justiciar (usually 12 senior men)
Everyone went to a gathering (court) where everyone would tell their story 
Over time, similar disputes were dealt with in the same way – Precedent and Common Law!

units.label: slide 11
units.text:
Punishment 
Prison/Jail weren’t used until the late 1500s
There were no juries and evidence was not important 
Trial by Ordeal – a physical test that determined guilt or innocence
Water, fire, hot water
If burn healed nicely, you were innocent
“To be in hot water”

units.label: slide 12
units.text:
Justice
We still use the term “ordeal” today
The verdicts were innocent and culpable – plea of not guilty was abbreviated cul. prist. 
Culprit (ready to be proven guilty)
If convicted for murder –death penalty, less serious crimes – sent away
Wergild  (lit. Man Money) was paid to the family of the deceased
Blood feuds were common before the wergild

units.label: slide 13
units.text:
Loopholes 
The church courts were the most lenient 
You had to prove you were a member of the clergy though
Pass a linguistic test in Latin and recite from the Book of Psalms 
Many would be criminals just memorized these passages…
“To get away with murder”

units.label: slide 14
units.text:
Turbulent Times
This period was very important for establishing roles and concepts that we still use today
There are other notable events prior to this that also impacted our legal system
Hammurabi’s Code 
“An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” 
The juries of ancient Greece and a blind Lady Justice
Solonian Constitution 
Romans and formation of Companies
